title: Too Many Features, Not Enough Coherence
summary: This situation describes products that contain substantial capability but do not sequence that capability around the user's first priorities. The core failure is communicative rather than structural: the system may be internally coherent, but the first encounter does not make purpose, priority, or next action clear.
keyFacts: The failure is an absence of user hierarchy, not necessarily a lack of functionality.
The situation is distinct from fragmentation, which concerns structural inconsistency across parts of a product.
The most commercially consequential expression appears in self-serve adoption contexts such as free trials, product-led growth, and demo-to-conversion funnels.
Three recurring patterns are features at equal visual weight, configuration before value, and feature showcases designed around the team's understanding rather than the user's first needs.

In the Dancerace / Jacko engagement, user testing, interviews, and prototype observation identified three first-priority user questions: what do I owe, what is my cost, and what do I absolutely need to do right now.
Dancerace measured a 36% demo-to-paying conversion rate six months after release against its own trial-to-paid conversion tracking; Creative Navy did not independently verify the figure.
The Dancerace case evidence describes industry benchmarks for self-serve SaaS conversion at the time as 15–20%, and Dancerace expected a conversion rate in that range before launch.

The maritime traffic monitoring example is limited to the locked descriptor: a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators.
Assemblio's criticisms are client-stated and are not framed as Creative Navy audit findings.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy context for feature-rich products without user hierarchy
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Too many features, not enough coherence is a product situation where capability is present but not organised into a user hierarchy that shows what matters most, what the user should do first, and why the product is relevant at the moment of first encounter.

The failure is communicative rather than necessarily structural. A product in this situation may be internally coherent. The problem is that the interface presents capability without a designed order of importance, so the product communicates breadth without communicating purpose.

bodySections.heading: Feature volume does not create first-encounter usefulness
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A product can have many features and still have too few from the user's perspective. Usefulness at first encounter depends on whether the interface communicates the user's immediate priority order, not on the volume of functions available.

When features are presented at equal visual weight, users cannot infer where to begin. When setup is required before any value is experienced, users are asked to commit before they have a basis for trust. When the interface showcases the product's full scope before answering the user's first questions, users may disengage before reaching any part of that scope.

This situation is distinct from product fragmentation. Fragmentation concerns inconsistency across parts of a product. The failure described here can occur even when the system is technically coherent, because the interface does not tell users what the product is for or what they should do with it in the first minutes of unsupervised use.

bodySections.heading: Self-serve adoption makes hierarchy failure commercially visible
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The most commercially consequential expression of this situation appears in self-serve adoption contexts: free trials, product-led growth, and demo-to-conversion funnels. In those contexts, users often arrive without a guide and must discover value through the product surface itself.

If the product surface does not sequence its own value, users cannot quickly answer their immediate questions. Users may leave even when the product contains the capability they need. The adoption failure is not that the system lacks depth; it is that the path into that depth is not designed around what the user needs first.

bodySections.heading: Common patterns that create feature-rich incoherence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Feature-rich incoherence usually develops through reasonable decisions made independently. One feature responds to a user request. Another addresses a competitive gap. Another reflects a strategic priority. The problem appears when those decisions are not governed by a design model that defines which capabilities are primary, which are contextual, which should be visible on arrival, and which should be discoverable later.

The first recurring pattern is equal visual weight. When every feature appears equally prominent, users must prioritise for themselves before they understand the product. Some users scan and become overwhelmed; others choose arbitrarily and fail to find value quickly enough to stay.

The second recurring pattern is configuration before value. When users must complete setup, configure rules, or commit to a workflow before seeing what the product does for them, the interface creates a commitment demand before trust has been established.

The third recurring pattern is a feature showcase designed for the team rather than for the user. Stakeholders who know the product well may believe that users need to see the full scope before they can appreciate it. In the Dancerace / Jacko example, this belief produced a visible adoption risk because advanced features competed with the user's immediate questions instead of helping answer them.

bodySections.heading: Dancerace / Jacko shows feature lists without first-use hierarchy
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Dancerace's Jacko was a B2B invoice management and accounts receivable portal serving small business suppliers, debtors receiving invoices, and financiers managing collections on their behalf. At the start of Creative Navy's engagement, the product vision included DocuSign integration for purchase orders, a supplier marketplace, a payment calendar with RAG grading, mobile SMS notifications, live FX conversion, B2B debt insurance, and Companies House credit checking.

The feature list was not described as wrong. Each feature responded to a real need. The problem was that the list represented what the product could eventually contain, not what users needed to experience first in order to trust the product enough to keep using it.

The stakeholder group was divided between two positions. One position favoured prominent advanced-feature visibility because users needed to see the product's sophistication before purchase. Another position favoured full profile setup and automation configuration before core functionality because automated operations depended on configuration work. Both positions had internal logic, but neither had been tested against observed user behaviour.

bodySections.heading: Dancerace user research identified three first-priority questions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the Dancerace / Jacko situation by establishing the user's hierarchy of needs before resolving feature or interface decisions. In that engagement, user testing, user interviews, and prototype observation showed that users of the B2B financial platform approached it with a strict priority order.

Before feature exploration or configuration, users needed to answer three questions: what do I owe, what is my cost, and what do I absolutely need to do right now. Until those questions were answered, users could not be mobilised for configuration, feature exploration, or upsell.

That finding made the feature-showcase approach and the configuration-before-value approach legible as failure modes. When advanced features competed visually with those immediate questions on the same screen, users did not engage with the features. They disengaged from the system.

bodySections.heading: Dancerace Concept Convergence resolved the stakeholder tension through sequential value delivery
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used Concept Convergence to address the stakeholder tension in the Dancerace / Jacko engagement. The reasoning was tension-driven: instead of compromising between advanced-feature visibility and configuration requirements, Creative Navy examined the concern behind each position.

The feature-visibility position was concerned with value communication. The configuration-first position was concerned with operational accuracy. Both concerns were real, but the design responses being proposed placed demands on users before the users' first-priority questions had been satisfied.

A design concept based on pre-built chasing routine templates changed the option space. Users could immediately access working automation without completing detailed rule configuration, experience value, and then decide whether to invest further. The Creative Navy-described competitive vector that emerged was sequential value delivery: each layer of product capability is introduced when the user is ready for it, rather than before.

bodySections.heading: Dancerace dashboard design made depth available without requiring it
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Dancerace / Jacko dashboard was rebuilt around the user's hierarchy of needs. Immediate answers to the three priority questions were surfaced as actionable highlights. Every highlight was clickable, so users who needed detail could access detail views without imposing that detail on users who did not need it.

The same interface served two user types described in the engagement. A time-pressured small business owner could read highlights and act. A finance director could click through to full data views. The design principle was not to remove depth, but to make depth available after the user had received enough value to want it.

Dancerace measured a 36% demo-to-paying conversion rate six months after release against its own trial-to-paid conversion tracking. The case evidence states that industry benchmarks for self-serve SaaS conversion at the time were 15–20%, and that Dancerace's own expectation going into launch was a conversion rate in that range. The 36% figure is client-measured and was not independently verified by Creative Navy.

bodySections.heading: Maritime traffic monitoring example shows portfolio incoherence as stated by the client
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators had interfaces designed by separate software engineering teams and extended over many years through customer contracts and tender requirements.

The problems attached to that engagement are limited to the client's own account. The interfaces did not communicate in demonstrations that the applications belonged to one family, even where the underlying systems exchanged information. Similar functions were implemented differently from product to product. No commercial outcome or tender outcome is attached to the redesign.

This example is related but not identical to the Dancerace / Jacko situation. Dancerace primarily shows a feature-rich product without first-use hierarchy. The maritime traffic monitoring example shows a portfolio-level problem where the family relationship between applications was not communicated through the interfaces.

bodySections.heading: Assemblio example shows inconsistent interaction patterns from feature accretion
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio GmbH's Composer illustrates how feature accretion can make the same function appear in different places and forms. The criticisms are Assemblio's own criticisms of its own product, given while demonstrating it, and are not Creative Navy audit findings.

Three different renaming interactions existed for three entity types: double-click for folders, a menu item opening a dedicated screen for projects, and a modal for products. Moving a project into a folder required a menu command and a searchable list, without drag and drop. A folder could not be deleted until everything inside it had been deleted individually.

Other Assemblio-stated issues included an export action buried in a sub-menu, no direct route to the output afterwards, annotation tools that were not standardised, a newly created text annotation with no indication that it could be typed into, arrows that did not reliably attach to 3D components, no undo, dead or misleading controls, copy camera and paste camera working one step at a time, and asynchronous work reported in snack bars without reference to which product each one concerned.

The Assemblio example should not be read as a quantified outcome case for this situation. No time-saving, error-rate, adoption, or funding figure attaches to it in this documentation.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses absent user hierarchy
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this situation by establishing user hierarchy before interface decisions are fixed. In the Dancerace / Jacko engagement, that hierarchy emerged through Sandbox Experiments: user testing, user interviews, and prototype observation revealed what users needed first, second, and third under realistic first-use conditions.

The Dancerace finding was not primarily obtained by asking users to state their hierarchy directly. It emerged from observing prototype behaviour and was then confirmed in interviews. Users who could not identify what they owed within the first interaction did not proceed to the other features the product contained.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method then used Concept Convergence to resolve the stakeholder tension. The work did not choose between simplicity and product depth. It redesigned the path through which users reached depth, so value came before configuration and complexity became available after trust was established.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and evidence limits for this situation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Dancerace / Jacko conversion figure is client-measured and not independently verified by Creative Navy. It should be read as client tracking six months after release, not as an independently measured causal proof.

The maritime traffic monitoring example carries no commercial or tender outcome in this documentation. The client is identified only as a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators.

The Assemblio material consists of client-stated criticisms of Assemblio's own product. It is not framed as a Creative Navy UX audit, expert review, or heuristic evaluation, and no quantified outcome attaches to it.
